compression.title: Data Portraits
compression.lede: is a 2023 proposal by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme (Johns Hopkins) for artifacts that record a model's training data so that a query can test whether an example was in it: a Bloom-filter sketch of hashed 50-character spans, built for The Pile and The Stack; it answers membership and nothing more, and the census finds in its record neither the name of a recorded work nor what a model made from it.

sentences.text: Data Portraits are artifacts that record the data a foundation model is trained on and allow that data to be inspected afterwards: proposed for widespread adoption in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University, and served as front ends over data sketches at dataportraits.org, which describes itself as "Dataset documentation through membership testing."

The question a portrait answers is whether a model has already encountered a given example during training, a question that grows difficult as models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets; its unit is a single example queried against a portrait of a training dataset.

Its critical property is membership inference, whether an example was part of a data collection, and its implementation supports membership testing and nothing more; its readback is a membership query against the recorded dataset.

The paper's conclusion restates the object as records supporting membership inference on the data used to train a model, and calls on dataset and model creators to release some form of Data Portrait as part of their essential documentation.
Its makers place it beside existing data and model documentation artifacts, datasheets and model cards among them, as a complementary artifact that answers the membership question.

The archive holds datasheets and model cards to be documentation norms for machine-learning artifacts as such, a training corpus being the instrument's experimental input, and reads training data as semantic capital, the datasheet proposal as a step toward the accounting that capital demands.

A portrait is a data sketch, a compressed and approximate view of data: the paper outlines the properties a membership tool should have (fast, lightweight, avoiding redistribution, local, indexing, flexible matching), weighs grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays against them, and chooses a probabilistic approach, built for fast and space-efficient querying.

The sketch is a Bloom filter, which stores only the hash of each element and can give false positives but never false negatives, filled with character n-grams of length 50 tiled across the corpus, a span the authors find already a good document fingerprint; tiling saves space at the risk of missing a string split by a tile boundary.
Since only hashes are distributed, a portrait gives some obfuscation of the recorded text, and a proprietary provider could in principle release one without revealing its exact training data.
The Pile's portrait takes 27 GB on disk with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, and its makers call the tool lightweight and fast, costing about 3% of the dataset's size in overhead.

Portraits were built for The Pile, a language-modelling corpus, as a 50-character n-gram sketch, and for The Stack, BigCode's code dataset, whose subset used to train StarCoder the Stack portrait documents exactly; the site also hosts a sketch of The Stack V2, code and text about code, and offers to build the system on other data, with its code on GitHub.
It is no corpus itself: it records corpora built by others.

The paper reports its solution answering questions of test-set leakage and model plagiarism: the Pile portrait shows that some machine-translation test data has leaked into the Pile, though whether a specific model memorized the translation targets cannot be concluded from it, and that XSum's summaries overlap the Pile most among the sets tested, with some LDC files apparently scraped into language-model corpora.

The Stack portrait powers a plagiarism check called from a code-completion plugin for StarCoder, which its makers call a lightweight first-pass check, further tools being needed to assess attribution.

Its makers write for three perspectives, content creators, scientists and content consumers, the creators wanting to know whether a dataset contains their content, and hope that a non-technical content creator could search for their material in a documented dataset.
The layer census records that it answers whether a given example is in a recorded dataset, and questions of leakage and plagiarism against it.
On novel New York Times text the Pile sketch gave no chained matches and a false positive rate of 7 × 10⁻⁴.
Its makers state its limits: few datasets studied, false positives, no retrieval of the context around a match, and the possibility that an open plagiarism detector is used to avoid detection.

The census, reading only the abstract, records no stated limit beyond the framing of opaque datasets, and lists what a portrait does not answer: whether a model's output depends causally on a recorded passage, under whose name a recorded example sits, and anything about a dataset with no portrait.
A portrait is no model-side test, since it queries the recorded data and needs a portrait of it, and in the census's reading dataset membership is no proof that a particular model used a passage.

The census reads a portrait as a readback instrument held on the corpus side, which settles for a recorded corpus whether a work is in the layer; the archive's field survey of training-layer literature states that the texts of the writers it surveys are, as a matter of fact, in the corpora.

On the model side the archive records membership inference attacks that can detect whether a trap sentence was in a training set, and distinguishability between models trained with and without a work that membership-inference research reports achievable against production-scale models, though unevenly across architectures, training procedures and defences.

The archive sets its own canary in a deposit, a phrase whose exact production by a model marks the document as present in that model's training corpus, and reads a membership attack that succeeds where a surfacing probe fails as an inscription that survived training and is suppressed at the output layer.

A portrait stores hashes of text spans; the census records the name of a recorded work as not recorded in its saved source, and the portrait as no record of authorship, its abstract saying nothing of attribution metadata.

In the archive's account of the training pipeline, author tags and copyright in a page's head are almost always discarded by the extractors that prepare text for training corpora, the body text and sometimes the URL retained, and no single author's style survives training as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified.

The archive's protocol for measuring training inscription counts metadata and labels within a work's provenance envelope, every training unit derived from the work, and its field survey makes persistence, placement where the training and retrieval layers look with the metadata that lets a work be found and attributed, a criterion of training-layer literature.

Every text in a training corpus, the archive holds, is semantic labour often unattributed; a training corpus without provenance is no commons; and provenance lost in unmarked augmentation passes downstream into the training corpus, where, preserved, it would let later pipelines distinguish the contribution of each stage.
What a model makes from a recorded work lies outside the portrait: the census records it as not recorded, the leakage and plagiarism checks being checks of material against the recorded data.

The archive's account of machine composition asks what a text makes possible for a machine to write, holds whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from to be different questions, sets what survived from a work beside what became possible because of it, and places the corpus within an institutional training loop in which a model's output enters the next corpus.
Machine reception, in the archive's field survey, is now partially measurable, since retrieval and rendering can be observed.

The paper appeared on arXiv on 6 March 2023, revised on 14 December 2023, in the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track; the census holds it as historical, a published paper, with the live interface and the paper's full text left unchecked.
On 1 November 2026 dataportraits.org served its landing page, while the front ends of its Pile, Stack and Stack V2 sketches answered HTTP 502.
The census sets it beside OLMoTrace, which matches verbatim spans against a full corpus where a portrait answers membership queries on a recorded one.

It enters the traininglayerliterature.org layer census as a method in the areas of inspection and the corpora, of the evidence kinds research paper and dataset documentation, with the relation of infrastructure, under the census's question of how literature addressed to a receiving apparatus can be inspected across later reception, its rule that an aggregator gathers and holds many records and says what it holds, and its anchors in #186 and #1543.

Three older senses of the name stay distinct entities: W. E. B. Du Bois's charts, graphs and maps for the 1900 Paris Exposition, made with Atlanta University students and scholars and published in full in 2018 as W. E. B. Du Bois's Data Portraits; Judith Donath's data portraits, "depictions of people made by visualizing data by and about them", which depict their subjects' accumulated data in place of their faces; and the Data Portraits Giorgia Lupi designed at Accurat for TED 2017, wearable buttons made from attendees' answers, more than 500 of them.
The encyclopedia has no article under the name, its variants or the paper's title, and its search for the phrase returns seven articles, the Du Bois book cited in several.

At the name, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed on 1 November 2026 a definition of data portraits as visual representations of people, four senses and an offer of three directions; the Capture Registry's innocent reading is that, given a two-word name that is also a term of visualization and portraiture, the Overview defines the term, lists its senses and asks which is meant.

The Registry finds the artifact the last of four senses and one card of eight, carried at a coarse grain as lightweight inspection tools that record dataset training traces, without its question, method, corpora, uses, authors or venue, while each other sense carries a person; it scores the reached kind a collision.
The page behind the artifact's card names the two authors and the venue in its citation, and calls the implementation "minimal and efficient" where the composition says lightweight.

It records a page under the name in the index that day, carrying the abstract's opening, where the census had left open whether the live interface is still served; that page is dataportraits.org, whose lead opens on the same question as the abstract.

CAP-1-07.quote: 'DATA PORTRAITS' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE TRAINING-DATA RECORD THE LAST OF FOUR SENSES, WITH NO AUTHOR, CORPUS OR QUESTION; DU BOIS, DONATH AND LUPI COMPOSED AROUND IT; A PAGE UNDER ITS NAME INDEXED

CAP-1-05.quote: The innocent reading first. Given a two-word name that is also a term of visualization and portraiture, the Overview defines the term, lists four senses of it and asks which the user means; the paper's artifact is the fourth.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE RECORD ONE SENSE OF FOUR. The paper's artifact holds the last bullet and one card of eight. The rest of the field is Du Bois's work for the Paris Exposition ('over 60 hand-drawn charts, graphs, and maps'), Donath's definition, carded from the MIT Media Lab ('Data portraits depict their subjects' accumulated data rather than their faces'), and Lupi's 'wearable buttons at TED 2017', carded twice (giorgialupi, Pentagram).

CAP-1-02.quote: THE ARTIFACT AT A COARSE GRAIN. 'lightweight inspection tools ... that record dataset training traces.' The abstract: 'artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection' and 'Our tool is lightweight and fast, costing only 3% of the dataset size in overhead.' The recording and the lightness are carried; 'training traces' is the composition's phrase. The question the artifact answers ('has the model already encountered a given example during training?'), its method ('a solution based on data sketching'), the two corpora it documents ('The Pile' and 'The Stack') and its uses ('test set leakage and model plagiarism') are absent.

CAP-1-03.quote: NO AUTHOR, NO VENUE. 'Contemporary research groups use the term': the abstract's authors, 'Marc Marone , Benjamin Van Durme', and its venue, 'NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks', are not named, and the sense is undated. Each of the other three senses carries a person ('Sociologist W. E. B. Du Bois', 'Digital media scholar Judith Donath', 'Designers like Giorgia Lupi').

CAP-1-06.quote: A disambiguation in which the training-data record is the last of four senses, named by the term alone with no author, venue, corpus or question. The membership query the census row reads it for, whether a work is in a recorded corpus, is not carried.

CAP-1-08.quote: Neither author of the paper nor any institution named for the artifact; a page under its name carded once among seven sources of the other senses.

CAP-1-10.quote: reached: Contemporary research groups use the term for lightweight inspection tools; The paper's artifact reached as the last of four senses of the name, beside Du Bois's charts, Donath's portraits and Lupi's TED project; one card of eight is its page.

CAP-1-04.quote: A PAGE UNDER THE NAME INDEXED. The second card, titled 'Data Portraits' under the site name 'Data Portraits', carries the abstract's opening ('Foundation models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets. Even while these models are now key in AI system building, it can be difficult to ans...'), and the composition's one link on the artifact goes to it. The census row records the 'live interface' as released and unread, and its lifecycle leaves open 'whether the live interface is still served'; on 2026-11-01 a page under the name is in the index, at an address the paste does not show.
